title: Investigating Role of Electron Correlation Effects via Triple Excitations for Precise Evaluation of Energies and Hyperfine Structure Constants in $^{23}$Na
abstract: Accurate determination of hyperfine structure constants in atomic systems provides important insight into the interplay of electron correlation and relativistic effects in the nuclear region. Although sodium (Na) is a relatively light atom, previous all-order relativistic many-body calculations of the magnetic dipole hyperfine constants for the low-lying states of $^{23}$Na show noticeable discrepancies with experiment. To address this, we calculate the ionization potentials and hyperfine structure constants of $^{23}$Na using relativistic coupled-cluster theory with explicit inclusion of triple excitations. We further incorporate corrections from the Breit interaction, quantum electrodynamics, and the Bohr-Weisskopf (BW) effect. Results from lower-order methods are also presented to assess the importance of different physical contributions across states. Our calculations demonstrate that contributions from the lower-order relativistic and BW effects play almost similar roles with the electron correlation effects, including triple excitations, and are essential for reconciling theoretical predictions with experimental observations. This study can also serve as a useful guide for understanding the role of triples in heavier alkali systems.
summary: The authors perform highly accurate relativistic many-body calculations on $^{23}	ext{Na}$ to predict its hyperfine structure constants. They systematically incorporate electron correlation effects up to triple excitations and include QED/Breit corrections. The findings emphasize that achieving experimental accuracy requires the combined inclusion of these higher-order correlation terms alongside fundamental physical interactions.
main_problem: The primary goal is to accurately determine hyperfine structure constants (HFCs) and ionization potentials for $^{23}	ext{Na}$ by rigorously investigating the role of electron correlation effects, particularly those involving triple excitations.
main_result: Accurate theoretical predictions require the inclusion of higher-order correlation terms (like triples), alongside relativistic corrections (Breit, QED, BW) to reconcile discrepancies between theory and experiment for $	ext{A}_{	ext{hf}}$.
method: The study employs advanced relativistic coupled-cluster theory ($	ext{RCCSDT}$) combined with perturbation theory treatments for various physical interactions.
model_or_system: The system is the sodium ($^{23}	ext{Na}$) atom. Calculations utilize a Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonian and treat electron correlation effects systematically through methods like $	ext{RMBPT}$ and coupled-cluster expansions up to triple excitations.
key_observables: Magnetic dipole hyperfine structure constants ($	ext{A}_{	ext{hf}}$), electric quadrupole hyperfine structure constants ($	ext{B}_{	ext{hf}}$), and Ionization Potentials (IPs).
important_parameters: The relative importance of correlation effects versus Breit, QED, and Bohr-Weisskopf corrections is a key focus.
main_assumptions: The calculations rely on approximations inherent to many-body perturbation theory ($	ext{RMBPT}$) or coupled-cluster expansions ($	ext{RCC}$), which systematically treat electron interactions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the systematic inclusion of different physical processes (e.g., correlation effects) and show how triple excitations modify $	ext{A}_{	ext{hf}}$ constants, while tables present numerical comparisons across various theoretical approximations.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares results from lower-order methods ($	ext{RMBPT}(2)$, RPA) against higher-order treatments incorporating explicit triple excitations ($	ext{RCCSDT}$), while also adding external corrections like Breit and QED to achieve convergence toward experimental values.
why_interesting: This work exemplifies the state-of-the-art in high-precision atomic structure theory, demonstrating how subtle correlation effects (like triples) are essential for matching spectroscopic measurements in alkali atoms.
